mainTopic: When late proof can overturn a ruling, and which court a case must go to
overview: The עמוד opens by finishing the discussion of a שליש (trustee). רב נחמן said a confirmed שטר cannot be weakened by the argument 'she could have burned it.' רבא challenges him from a ברייתא about a receipt, and רב נחמן is refuted. Next, the גמרא asks when a losing litigant may still bring new proof. רב דימי's report of רבי יוחנן is rejected. רב שמואל בר יהודה's version stands: once he told בית דין 'I have no witnesses, no proof,' he is blocked, unless the proof was something he could not have known about. Then the גמרא discusses whether a case is heard locally or at the central court (מקום הוועד). רבי אלעזר rules it stays local, the יבמה travels to the יבם for חליצה, and אמימר concludes that a lender can demand the central court while a borrower cannot. The עמוד ends with a letter to מר עוקבא, two explanations of its wording, and the הדרן closing פרק זה בורר.

steps.title: She could have burned it
steps.stepSummary: This word finishes רבא's challenge: the trustee should be believed, because she could have burned the שטר.
steps.simpleTranslation: [If she had wanted, she could have] burned it!
steps.whatsHappening: This one word ends רבא's question from just before. He asks רב נחמן why the woman holding the שטר was not believed, since she could have destroyed it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The argument is a kind of מיגו. Destroying the שטר would have hurt the lender even more than her statement does. So if she wanted to lie, she had an easier way to do it, and she should be believed. The question sets up רב נחמן's answer in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: If she had wanted, she could have burned it
A trustee, a third party holding a document for both sides

phrases.english: she could have burned it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבא's challenge, which began before this section.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's ruling not to believe the trustee
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: She had the power to destroy the שטר, so her lesser claim should be believed.

steps.title: A confirmed שטר is not weakened by 'she could have burned it'
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן answers that once a שטר is confirmed in בית דין, the argument 'she could have burned it' does not work.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the שטר was confirmed in court, we do not say 'if she had wanted, she could have burned it.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן defends his ruling. The שטר had already been confirmed by בית דין, so the trustee's word cannot take away its strength.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שטר that בית דין has confirmed (קיום) has a strong legal standing. The fact that she was physically able to burn it does not give her words the power to cancel it. Without real evidence, a confirmed שטר stays valid.

keyTerms.meaning: Was established or confirmed
The court (בית דין)
We do not say (we do not apply this reasoning)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a court's confirmation can block a מיגו based only on what someone was physically able to do.

phrases.english: Since it was confirmed in court,
phrases.notes: 'It' is the שטר. Once בית דין confirms the signatures, the document is on solid ground.

phrases.english: we do not say 'if she wanted, she could have burned it.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's challenge in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the reasoning: the 'she could have burned it' argument does not apply to a שטר confirmed in court.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The trustee's ability to destroy the שטר should make her believed.
steps.terutzMaskana: After a שטר is confirmed in בית דין, her ability to burn it does not make her believed.

steps.title: A ברייתא shows a trustee is believed about a receipt
steps.stepSummary: רבא brings a ברייתא: a receipt with no witnesses is still valid if it comes out of a trustee's hands. So a שליש is believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא objected to רב נחמן: A receipt that has witnesses signed on it is confirmed through its signers. If it has no witnesses, but it came out of the hands of a trustee, or it was written below the signatures of the שטר, it is valid. So a trustee is believed!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks again, this time with a ברייתא about a receipt (סימפון). The ברייתא says a receipt that comes from a trustee is valid even without witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A receipt says the debt was paid, so it weakens the שטר, just like the woman's claim did. The ברייתא accepts it based only on the trustee, which shows the trustee is trusted. That contradicts רב נחמן's ruling that the trustee is not believed.

keyTerms.meaning: A receipt saying a debt was paid
Its signers (the witnesses who signed it)
The signing of the documents (the witnesses' signatures on the שטר)
So it seems, apparently

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two documents. The שטר is the loan document; the סימפון is the receipt that cancels it. The ברייתא is about the receipt.

phrases.english: Rava raised an objection to Rav Nachman:
A receipt that has witnesses on it
is confirmed through its signers.
If it has no witnesses on it,
but it came out of the hands of a trustee,
or it appears after the signatures of the document,
it is valid.
So apparently a trustee is believed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רב נחמן's answer, רבא brings a new challenge from a ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's ruling that the trustee is not believed
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא accepts a receipt only because a trustee held it, which shows a trustee's word is trusted even against a שטר.

steps.title: רב נחמן's view is refuted
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that the ברייתא is a full refutation of רב נחמן.
steps.simpleTranslation: The refutation of רב נחמן is a conclusive refutation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives no answer to רבא's challenge and declares that רב נחמן's view is refuted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the ברייתא clearly trusts a שליש, רב נחמן's ruling cannot stand. The conclusion is that a trustee is believed.

keyTerms.meaning: A refutation, a challenge that has no answer

steps.whatToRemember: A שליש (trustee) is believed. רב נחמן's attempt to block the 'she could have burned it' argument for a confirmed שטר is refuted by the ברייתא about a receipt.

phrases.english: The refutation of Rav Nachman is a conclusive refutation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts רבא's challenge from step 3 as final.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב נחמן's ruling is rejected, and a שליש is believed.

steps.title: רב דימי's report of רבי יוחנן's rule on bringing new proof
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי reports that רבי יוחנן said a litigant can always bring proof to overturn a ruling, until his claims are stopped up and he says 'come, so-and-so, testify for me'.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב דימי came from ארץ ישראל, he said in the name of רבי יוחנן: a person can always bring proof and overturn the ruling, until his claims are stopped up and he says, 'Come, so-and-so and so-and-so, and testify for me.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins: רב דימי reports a rule from רבי יוחנן about when a losing litigant may still bring new proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The basic rule is generous: new proof can overturn a ruling. The limit is when the person's claims are 'stopped up'. In this version, that limit is defined by the case where he calls out 'come, so-and-so, testify for me', which looks like he is just making up witnesses after losing.

keyTerms.meaning: Brings proof and overturns the earlier ruling
That his claims are 'stopped up', meaning he has no more claims to make
'Come, so-and-so and so-and-so, and testify for me', a suspicious last-minute call for witnesses

phrases.english: When Rav Dimi came
he said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
One can always bring proof and overturn the ruling,
until his claims are stopped up
and he says: Come, so-and-so and so-and-so, and testify for me.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי, אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the שליש discussion ended with a refutation of רב נחמן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A litigant may always bring proof to overturn a ruling until his claims are stopped up, defined here as saying 'come, so-and-so, testify for me'.

steps.title: The report contradicts itself
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the first half of רבי יוחנן's statement follows the רבנן, while the second half follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.simpleTranslation: This statement itself is difficult. You said 'his claims are stopped up', which is the view of the רבנן. Then you said 'come, so-and-so, testify for me', which is the view of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב דימי's report because its two halves seem to follow two different opinions in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the רבנן say that once a person has run out of claims, he cannot bring proof later. רשב"ג limits the blocking to the suspicious case of 'come, so-and-so, testify for me'. One statement cannot follow both views at once.

keyTerms.meaning: 'This itself is difficult': the statement contradicts itself
'We have arrived at the רבנן': this matches the view of the Sages

phrases.english: This itself is difficult:
You said 'his claims are stopped up';
we have arrived at the view of the Rabbis,
phrases.notes: The רבנן in our משנה, who say that once he ran out of claims, later proof does not help.

phrases.english: and then you said
'Come, so-and-so and so-and-so, and testify for me';
we have arrived at the view of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the internal consistency of רב דימי's report in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב דימי's version of רבי יוחנן's statement
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The first clause matches the רבנן and the second matches רשב"ג, so the statement mixes two opposing views.

steps.title: Suggestion: the whole statement follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the whole statement is רשב"ג's view, with the second half explaining what 'claims stopped up' means.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say the whole statement follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, and רבי יוחנן is just explaining himself: what does 'until his claims are stopped up' mean? Until he says, 'Come, so-and-so and so-and-so, and testify for me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proposes a way to fix the contradiction: read the whole statement as רשב"ג. The very next step will knock this idea down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On this reading, 'claims stopped up' is not the רבנן's idea at all. It is only a name for the 'come, testify for me' case. That would make the statement consistent, as long as רבי יוחנן really rules like רשב"ג.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And if you would say': introduces a possible answer, usually about to be rejected
'He is explaining': the second clause explains the first

phrases.english: And if you would say:
the whole statement follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel,
and he is explaining himself:
What does 'until his claims are stopped up' mean?

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁיֹּאמַר: קִרְבוּ פְּלוֹנִי וּפְלוֹנִי וְהַעִידוּנִי.
phrases.english: Until he says: Come, so-and-so and so-and-so, and testify for me.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא: כּוּלַּהּ רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a possible resolution to the contradiction raised in step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the statement so both clauses follow one opinion
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two clauses follow two different תנאים.
steps.terutzMaskana: The second clause only explains the first, so everything follows רשב"ג.

steps.title: Objection: רבי יוחנן does not rule like רשב"ג here
steps.stepSummary: The suggestion fails because רבי יוחנן himself said the הלכה follows רשב"ג everywhere in the משנה except three cases, and this case is one of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: wherever רבן שמעון בן גמליאל taught something in our משנה, the הלכה follows him, except for the guarantor, צידן, and the last proof.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the suggestion from step 7 by quoting another rule of רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'The last proof' is the very dispute about late proof in our משנה. רבי יוחנן says the הלכה does not follow רשב"ג there. So he could not have stated a rule that is entirely רשב"ג, and רב דימי's report still has a problem.

keyTerms.meaning: The הלכה follows his view
A guarantor on a loan, one of the three exceptions
צידן, a city where a story in the משנה took place, another exception
'The last proof': the dispute in our משנה about bringing proof late

steps.whyThisMatters: This famous rule, that the הלכה follows רשב"ג in the משנה except in three places, is used throughout ש"ס.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה
phrases.english: But didn't Rabba bar bar Chana say
that Rabbi Yochanan said:
Anywhere that
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel taught in our Mishnah,
the halacha follows him,
except for the guarantor, Tzaidan, and the last proof?
phrases.notes: 'The last proof' is exactly our case, so here the הלכה follows the רבנן, not רשב"ג.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Knocks down the answer offered in step 7.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The suggestion that רבי יוחנן's whole statement follows רשב"ג
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רבי יוחנן himself rules against רשב"ג in the case of 'the last proof', so he would not state a rule that follows רשב"ג.

steps.title: The correct report: רב שמואל בר יהודה's version
steps.stepSummary: Instead, רב שמואל בר יהודה reports that רבי יוחנן blocks late proof only after the litigant said 'I have no witnesses, I have no proof'. Witnesses from overseas or a found bag of his father's papers can still overturn the ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, when רב שמואל בר יהודה came, he said in the name of רבי יוחנן: a person can always bring proof and overturn the ruling, until his claims are stopped up. That means the judges told him 'bring witnesses' and he said 'I have no witnesses', and 'bring proof' and he said 'I have no proof'. But if witnesses came from overseas, or his father's bag of papers was deposited with someone else, he can bring that proof and overturn the ruling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops רב דימי's version and replaces it with a different report of what רבי יוחנן said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here 'claims stopped up' means he told בית דין he had no witnesses and no proof. That fits the רבנן, so it agrees with רבי יוחנן's rule against רשב"ג. Even so, if the new proof is something he truly could not have known about or reached, like witnesses abroad or papers held by someone else, he may still use it.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Rather': the earlier version is dropped and a new one is offered
'Bring witnesses': בית דין's demand to the litigant
Overseas, a faraway land
A bag or case for storing documents
Deposited, left in someone's keeping

steps.whatToRemember: The accepted version of רבי יוחנן follows the רבנן: once you told בית דין 'I have no witnesses, I have no proof', you are blocked. But proof you could not have known about, like witnesses from overseas or your father's papers held by someone else, can still overturn the ruling.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix the two versions. רב דימי's version, which links 'claims stopped up' to 'come, so-and-so, testify for me', was rejected. רב שמואל בר יהודה's version is the one that stands.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא, כִּי אֲתָא רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר יְהוּדָה,
phrases.english: Rather, when Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda came,
he said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
One can always bring proof and overturn the ruling,
until his claims are stopped up
and they say to him: 'Bring witnesses,'
and he says: 'I have no witnesses.'
'Bring proof,' and he says: 'I have no proof.'
But if witnesses came from overseas,
or if there was a bag of his father's papers
deposited with someone else,
he may bring that proof and overturn the ruling.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, כִּי אֲתָא רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר יְהוּדָה, אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Since רב דימי's version fell apart in steps 6 to 8, the גמרא replaces it with a different report of רבי יוחנן's words.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replacing a flawed report with a different version of the same teacher's words
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוחנן linked 'claims stopped up' to the 'come, testify for me' case, which mixes the רבנן and רשב"ג.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יוחנן follows the רבנן: he is blocked after saying 'I have no witnesses or proof', except for proof he truly could not have known about.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: the case goes to the central court
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי reports that רבי יוחנן said: if one litigant wants to be judged locally and the other wants the central court (מקום הוועד), the one who wants the local court is forced to go to the central court.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב דימי came, he said that רבי יוחנן says: One person is pressing another in a court case. One says, 'Let's be judged here,' and the other says, 'Let's go to the place of the Assembly.' We force him to go to the place of the Assembly.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new topic with a ruling from רבי יוחנן. It is about which court hears a case when the two sides disagree on where to go.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two choices: the local court or the central court. In this report, the side that wants the central court wins, and the other side is forced to travel there.

keyTerms.meaning: When [he] came (a sage arriving from ארץ ישראל to בבל with a teaching)
One who presses his fellow in a court case
The place of the Assembly, meaning the big central court
We force him

phrases.english: When Rav Dimi came,
he said that Rabbi Yochanan says:
One who presses his fellow in a court case,
one says, "Let us be judged here,"
and one says, "Let us go to the place of the Assembly" —
phrases.notes: The big central court, not the local court in town.

phrases.english: we force him, and he goes to the place of the Assembly.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי, אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion of late proof ended in step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the litigants disagree on the court, the one who wants the local court is forced to go to the central court.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר objects: spending a hundred to collect a hundred
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר challenges רבי יוחנן: if the central court is required, a man owed a מנה would have to spend a מנה on the trip just to collect it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said before him: My teacher, if someone is owed a מנה by his fellow, should he have to spend a מנה to collect that מנה?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר, רבי יוחנן's student, attacks the ruling from step 10. He shows that it leads to an unfair result.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Travel to the central court costs money. If either side could force a trip there, the cost could equal the whole debt, so going to court would be pointless. The ruling cannot be right as stated.

keyTerms.meaning: He said before him (a student speaking to his teacher)
Is owed a debt; a creditor
A coin worth one hundred זוז

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said before him:
My teacher, one who is owed a maneh by his fellow,
should he spend a maneh for a maneh?
phrases.notes: He means the cost of the trip and lodging could be as much as the debt itself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling of step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's ruling that the side who wants the local court is forced to go to the central court.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It leads to an absurd result: the travel cost could equal the debt, so a creditor would gain nothing by going to court.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר's correction: the case is judged in the local city
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר replaces the ruling with the opposite one: the side who wants the central court is forced to be judged locally.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, we force him, and he is judged in his own city.
steps.whatsHappening: After his objection, רבי אלעזר gives the ruling he thinks is correct. The case stays in the local town.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אלא ("rather") flips the result. Now the one who wanted the central court is forced to accept the local court, so nobody spends a fortune on travel.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (introduces a corrected ruling)
Is judged in his own city

steps.confusionAlert: Both step 10 and step 12 say כופין אותו ("we force him"), but they mean different people. In step 10 the one who wanted the local court is forced to travel. Here the one who wanted the central court is forced to stay local.

phrases.english: Rather, we force him, and he is judged in his own city.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the problem from step 11 by reversing the ruling of step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Correction of the ruling: the opposite outcome is the right one.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The side who wants the central court can force the other side to travel there.
steps.terutzMaskana: The side who wants the central court is forced to be judged in the local city.

steps.title: רב ספרא's version supports the local court
steps.stepSummary: רב ספרא reports רבי יוחנן's statement in a form that matches רבי אלעזר: the one who wants the central court is forced to be judged locally.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also stated: רב ספרא said that רבי יוחנן says: Two people are struggling in a court case. One says, 'Let's be judged here,' and the other says, 'Let's go to the place of the Assembly.' We force him, and he is judged in his own city.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another report of רבי יוחנן's teaching. This version agrees with רבי אלעזר's corrected ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words איתמר נמי ("it was also stated") show support. Through רב ספרא, רבי יוחנן himself is reported as ruling that the case stays local. This backs up רבי אלעזר's correction of רב דימי's report.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also stated (brings support from another report)
Were struggling in a court case; each side digging in

steps.whatToRemember: רב ספרא's report backs רבי אלעזר: when the two sides disagree, the case is heard in the local city. Later, אמימר limits this to a borrower who asks for the central court (see step 22).
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical rule: the local court has the power to hear the case, which protects people from heavy travel costs.

phrases.english: It was also stated:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב סָפְרָא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rav Safra says that Rabbi Yochanan says:
Two who were struggling in a court case,
one says, "Let us be judged here,"
and one says, "Let us go to the place of the Assembly" —
we force him, and he is judged in his own city.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר נָמֵי: אָמַר רַב סָפְרָא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי אלעזר's ruling from step 12 with a different report of רבי יוחנן's words.
steps.raayaObject: The ruling that the case is judged in the local city.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב ספרא's report of רבי יוחנן's teaching.

steps.title: The local court may write to the higher court with questions
steps.stepSummary: Continuing רב ספרא's report: if the local court needs to ask about something, it writes to the central court, and the answer is sent back.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if a matter needs to be asked, they write, and an answer is sent.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ספרא's report adds a detail to the ruling. The case stays local, but the local court can still get help from the higher court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answers a possible worry that the local court may not know enough. The case stays local, and only a letter travels, so the litigants get the higher court's knowledge without the travel cost.

keyTerms.meaning: A matter needed to be asked
They write and send

phrases.english: And if a matter needed to be asked —
phrases.notes: The local court is the one with the question, and it asks the central court.

phrases.english: they write, and they send.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a procedural detail to the local-court ruling of step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the local court is unsure, it writes to the central court and receives a written answer.

steps.title: A litigant may ask for the court's reasons in writing
steps.stepSummary: If a litigant asks the court to write down why it ruled as it did, the judges write it and give it to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he says, 'Write down for what reason you judged me, and give it to me,' they write it and give it to him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ספרא's report of רבי יוחנן continues with another rule about the local court. A litigant can ask for a written explanation of the ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being judged locally does not leave a litigant without protection. With the written reasons, he can check the ruling or show it to the higher court.

keyTerms.meaning: For what reason
You judged me
They write it and give it to him

phrases.english: And if he says:
"Write and give me
for what reason you judged me" —
they write it and give it to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם אָמַר: כִּתְבוּ וּתְנוּ לִי מֵאֵיזֶה טַעַם דַּנְתּוּנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a further rule about the local court's procedure.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A litigant who asks for the court's reasoning in writing must be given it.

steps.title: The יבמה goes to the יבם's town for חליצה
steps.stepSummary: A new rule about location: a יבמה must go to where her brother-in-law (the יבם) is, so that he can release her.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the יבמה goes after the יבם, to his place, so he can release her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another rule about where a legal act happens: the widow goes to the brother-in-law, not the other way around.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The topic is still 'whose town do we go to?'. Here the answer is clear: the יבם stays put, and the יבמה must travel to his town for the חליצה that frees her to remarry.

keyTerms.meaning: A widow whose husband died without children, who is tied to his brother
The brother of the man who died, who must either marry the widow or release her
To release her, through חליצה, so she can marry someone else

phrases.english: And the widow tied to her brother-in-law
goes after the brother-in-law, for him to release her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a related rule about the location of a legal process, like the earlier rules about which court a case goes to.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The יבמה must travel to the יבם's place for חליצה.

steps.title: How far must she travel?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how far the יבמה has to go to reach the יבם.
steps.simpleTranslation: Up to how far?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question to set up the next line: is there a limit to how far she must travel?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule in Step 16 sounds like it could be a big burden. The question asks whether there is a limit on the distance or the type of place.

keyTerms.meaning: Up to how far / up to what point?

phrases.english: Up to how far?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the limits of the rule just stated.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How far the יבמה must travel to the יבם.

steps.title: Even from טבריא to ציפורי
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי answers that she must travel even from טבריא to ציפורי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אמי said: even from טבריא to ציפורי.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי answers the question: she must go even from טבריא to ציפורי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word "even" shows this is a real stretch. טבריא was the more important center, yet she still has to leave it and go to the יבם's town of ציפורי.

keyTerms.meaning: Even
טבריא, an important city with a major court
ציפורי, another city in the גליל

phrases.english: Rabbi Ami said:
Even from Tiberias to Tzippori.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַמֵּי: אֲפִילּוּ מִטְּבֶרְיָא לְצִפּוֹרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: She must go even from טבריא to ציפורי. She does not get to stay in the more important city.

steps.title: The פסוק says the elders of HIS city
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא brings the source: the Torah says the elders of his city call him, not the elders of her city.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: what is the פסוק? "And the elders of his city shall call him", and not the elders of her city.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא gives the Torah source for the rule that the יבמה goes to the יבם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about חליצה says the elders of "his" city deal with him. Since it does not say "her" city, the חליצה happens in his town, so she must come to him.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the פסוק (the source)?
The elders of his city

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said: What is the verse?
"And the elders of his city shall call him"
and not the elders of her city.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the Torah source for the rule in Steps 16 and 18.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that the יבמה travels to the יבם's town.
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברים 25:8, "the elders of his city", which means his city and not hers.

steps.title: אמימר: one can be forced to go to the central court
steps.stepSummary: אמימר rules that the litigant is forced to go to the place of the central court.
steps.simpleTranslation: אמימר said: the הלכה is that we force him to go to the place of the central court.
steps.whatsHappening: Going back to court cases, אמימר gives a final ruling: if one side wants the central court, the other side is forced to go there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This sounds like the first version of רבי יוחנן, the one רבי אלעזר rejected in Steps 11-12. So אמימר's ruling looks like it clashes with what we already learned.

keyTerms.meaning: The final practical ruling (הלכה)
We force him
The place of the central court (the main gathering of the sages)

phrases.english: Ameimar said: The halakha is
we force him, and he goes to the place of the central court.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַמֵּימָר: הִילְכְתָא, כּוֹפִין אוֹתוֹ וְיֵלֵךְ לִמְקוֹם הַוַּועַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the topic of which court a case goes to, after the side point about the יבמה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A litigant can be forced to go to the central court.

steps.title: רב אשי: but רבי אלעזר said to judge locally
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי challenges אמימר from רבי אלעזר's ruling that the litigant is forced to be judged in his own city.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said to אמימר: but רבי אלעזר said we force him to be judged in his own city!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי attacks אמימר's ruling by quoting the opposite ruling of רבי אלעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 12, רבי אלעזר said the side who wants the central court is forced to stay local. אמימר just said the opposite, so how can both be true?

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't he say...? (a challenge from an earlier statement)
And he is judged in his own city

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said to Ameimar:
But didn't Rabbi Elazar say:
We force him, and he is judged in his own city!
phrases.notes: This is רבי אלעזר's ruling from a few lines earlier (Step 12).

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: כּוֹפִין אוֹתוֹ וְדָן בְּעִירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges אמימר's ruling in Step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: אמימר's ruling that a litigant is forced to go to the central court.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי אלעזר ruled the opposite: the side wanting the central court is forced to be judged locally.

steps.title: It depends on who wants the trip: borrower or lender
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר's rule is when the borrower wants the central court. But the lender can demand it, because "the borrower is a servant to the lender."
steps.simpleTranslation: That rule is when the borrower says to the lender, 'let's go to the central court.' But if the lender wants it, then "the borrower is a servant to the lender."
steps.whatsHappening: אמימר answers that the two rulings are about different people: the borrower cannot drag the lender away, but the lender can make the borrower go.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר's worry (Step 11) was that a lender should not lose his money on travel just to collect a debt. So when the borrower asks for the central court, we keep the case local. When the lender asks, the borrower must go, as the פסוק says the borrower is like a servant to the lender.

keyTerms.meaning: These words apply only to... (limits a rule to a certain case)
Borrower
Lender

steps.whatToRemember: Both rulings stand: if the borrower wants the central court, he is forced to be judged locally (רבי אלעזר); if the lender wants the central court, the borrower is forced to go there (אמימר).
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think אמימר and רבי אלעזר really argue. Each one is talking about a different side asking for the trip.

phrases.english: These words apply where
phrases.notes: אמימר is answering רב אשי here.

phrases.english: the borrower says to the lender (let's go to the central court);
but if it is the lender (who wants to go),
"The borrower is a servant to the lender."

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנֵי מִילֵּי הֵיכָא דְּקָאָמַר לֵיהּ לֹוֶה לְמַלְוֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אשי's challenge in Step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the cases: different rules for borrower and lender.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It looked like אמימר and רבי אלעזר give opposite rulings on the same case.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי אלעזר's rule is when the borrower wants the central court; אמימר's rule is when the lender wants it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical הלכה: the lender can choose the central court, but the borrower cannot use it to make collecting the debt hard.

steps.title: The letter sent to מר עוקבא
steps.stepSummary: The Sages of ארץ ישראל write to מר עוקבא about עוקבן הבבלי's complaint against his brother ירמיה, saying 'tell him' and 'have him see us in טבריא.'
steps.simpleTranslation: They sent to מר עוקבא: To the one who shines like משה, peace. עוקבן the Babylonian complained to us: My brother ירמיה did me a great wrong. Tell him: make him come and see us in טבריא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a letter from the Sages of ארץ ישראל to מר עוקבא, the leader in בבל, about summoning a litigant to טבריא. This sets up the next step, where the גמרא will find a problem in the letter's wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This fits the topic we have been learning: can one side force the other to travel to a more important court? The letter seems to show a litigant being called all the way from בבל to טבריא. But its wording is unclear, and the גמרא will now examine it.

keyTerms.meaning: They sent to him (a letter)
To the one who has radiance (a title of honor)
Complained before us
Compel him (make him come)

phrases.english: They sent to Mar Ukva:
To the one who has radiance like the son of Bithiah, peace.
phrases.notes: 'The son of בתיה' is משה, who was raised by פרעה's daughter. It's a very honorable greeting.

phrases.english: Ukvan the Babylonian complained before us:

phrases.aramaic: יִרְמְיָה אָחִי הֶעֱבִיר עָלַי אֶת הַדֶּרֶךְ.
phrases.english: Yirmeya my brother passed the road over me.
phrases.notes: This is an expression. It means he did me a serious wrong.

phrases.english: Tell him:
Make him come, and he will see our face in Tiberias.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a real-life letter connected to the rule that a litigant can be made to go to the central court.
steps.raayaObject: Whether a litigant can be summoned from a local court to the main court in ארץ ישראל.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The letter from the Sages of ארץ ישראל to מר עוקבא.

steps.title: The letter seems to contradict itself
steps.stepSummary: 'Tell him' suggests the court in בבל should judge, but 'see us in טבריא' suggests sending him to ארץ ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: This letter itself is difficult. You said 'tell him,' which means: judge him yourselves. Then you said 'make him come to see us in טבריא,' which means: send him here.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the two halves of the letter seem to say opposite things.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Tell him' sounds like the Sages are giving the case to מר עוקבא to handle in בבל. But 'he should see our face in טבריא' sounds like they want the man sent to them. Which one did they mean?

keyTerms.meaning: This itself is difficult (it contradicts itself)
Apparently / this shows that
Judge him yourselves
Send him here

phrases.english: This itself is difficult:
You said 'Tell him,'
apparently: judge him yourselves.
'Make him come, and he will see our face in Tiberias,'
apparently: send him here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of the letter quoted in step 23.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The first half points to judging in בבל and the second half points to sending him to טבריא, so the letter contradicts itself.

steps.title: Judge him first, send him only if he refuses
steps.stepSummary: The letter means: judge him in בבל; if he obeys, good; if not, send him to טבריא.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what they meant: Tell him, judge him yourselves. If he listens, fine. If not, make him come see us in טבריא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that both halves of the letter are true, one after the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is no contradiction, because the two instructions are steps in order. First the court in בבל judges the case. Only if ירמיה refuses to obey is he sent to the Sages in טבריא.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what they meant
If he listens, he listens (fine)
And if not

phrases.english: (Rather,) this is what they were saying:
phrases.notes: The word in round brackets appears in the printed גמרא, but the corrected text leaves it out.

phrases.english: Tell him, meaning, judge him yourselves.
If he listens, he listens,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי לָא – הַשִּׂיאוּהוּ וְיִרְאֶה פָּנֵינוּ בִּטְבֶרְיָא.
phrases.english: and if not, make him come, and he will see our face in Tiberias.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the two parts as steps in order
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The letter gives two clashing instructions: judge locally, or send him away.
steps.terutzMaskana: Judge locally first; send him to טבריא only if he refuses to obey.

steps.title: רב אשי: it was a case of fines, which בבל cannot judge
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says the case involved דיני קנסות, which are not judged in בבל, so he had to be sent; 'tell him' was just to honor מר עוקבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: It was a case of fines, and in בבל they do not judge cases of fines. And the reason they wrote to him this way was to show honor to מר עוקבא.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a different answer to the contradiction: the case really had to go to ארץ ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רב אשי, the court in בבל could not judge this case at all, because it was about דיני קנסות (the background is that judges in בבל did not have סמיכה). So 'see us in טבריא' is the real instruction. 'Tell him' was not handing over the case; it was polite wording to honor מר עוקבא.

keyTerms.meaning: Cases of fines (penalties set by the Torah)
They do not judge
To show honor

steps.whatToRemember: Two answers to the letter: (1) judge in בבל first, and send to טבריא only if he refuses; (2) רב אשי: it was דיני קנסות, which בבל cannot judge, so he had to be sent, and 'tell him' was only to honor מר עוקבא.
steps.confusionAlert: In רב אשי's answer, 'tell him' does NOT mean מר עוקבא should judge the case. It is only a respectful way of writing.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
It was a case of fines,
and in Babylonia they do not judge cases of fines.
And the fact that they sent to him this way:
was in order to show honor to Mar Ukva.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: דִּינֵי קְנָסוֹת הֲוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different answer to the contradiction in step 24, instead of the answer in step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case so that only one half of the letter is the real instruction
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Tell him' meant the court in בבל should judge the case.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case could only be judged in ארץ ישראל; 'tell him' was polite wording for מר עוקבא's honor.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that cases of fines can only be judged in ארץ ישראל, and that the Sages took care to honor a leader even while giving him instructions.

steps.title: Hadran — Closing the chapter זה בורר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes the third פרק of סנהדרין, called זה בורר, with the traditional farewell formula.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, chapter 'זה בורר.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is not an argument. It is the closing line that marks the end of the פרק זה בורר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each פרק of the גמרא ends with הדרן עלך plus the פרק's name, which comes from its opening words. Here the name is זה בורר, from the first line of the משנה: 'This one chooses one judge.' The discussion about which court a case must go to, which ended with רב אשי's answer in step 26, is now complete.

keyTerms.meaning: 'We will return to you.' The farewell line said at the end of every פרק.
'This one chooses.' The name of this פרק, taken from its opening words about each side choosing a judge.
A chapter of the משנה and גמרא.

steps.whatToRemember: The פרק זה בורר covered how monetary cases are judged: choosing the judges, who is disqualified as a judge or witness, how the judges decide, and which court a case belongs in. Near the end, the גמרא ruled that a lender can demand the central court but a borrower cannot. It closed with the letter to מר עוקבא.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't look for a new הלכה or argument in this line. It is only a marker that the פרק is over.

phrases.english: We will return to you,
phrases.notes: This is a promise to come back and learn this פרק again.

phrases.english: chapter 'This one chooses.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the פרק right after רב אשי's explanation of the letter to מר עוקבא.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The פרק זה בורר is complete. Learning moves on to the next פרק.
